newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EMU voting dynamics may give Britain a key role.
newsitem.headline: EMU voting dynamics may give Britain a key role.

text.p: Although Britain is unlikely to take part in the launching of a single European currency, its views on the candidates scrambling for entry could be critical to their chances of success.
Despite securing an opt-out to the euro during negotiations on the Maastricht Treaty, Britain will still have a say on whether each country has met the criteria for monetary union.
In the complex game of EU voting, Britain can, by its sheer voting weight, alter the fate for any number of countries, particularly if it is able to rally a few additional members to its side.

What Britain thinks about Italy, for example, may be just as important as Germany's views. Both countries have 10 votes in the European Union. The only other countries with a similar number are France and Italy.

Rounding out the list, Spain follows with eight votes, while the Netherlands, Belgium, Greece and Portugal have five each. Sweden and Austria get four a piece. Denmark, Ireland and Finland are allotted only three each and tiny Luxembourg wields the least power in the bloc with just two votes.

The total comes to 87 and under the Treaty's so-called qualified majority voting procedure, 62 are needed for a country to join the euro. Meanwhile, at least 26 votes -- including absentions -- and six members are needed to reject an applicant.
The number of permutations and voting blocs that might emerge from this process could, therefore, give Britain a very influential role.
Among the scenarios that one can come up with, analysts say several are straightforward.

For example, a small core group of countries joining EMU -- say, Germany, France, Luxembourg, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria -- could not be formed if southern European nations voted as a bloc against this grouping.
Italy, Spain, Portugal and Greece together have 28 votes.
Similarly, a core EMU group voting together -- which might include Ireland or Finland but not Belgium, for example -- could also block any other country from joining.
Under what is now considered as the most likely outcome, a broad EMU with potentially 11 nations joining in 1999, the votes of Britain and Denmark and Sweden come into sharper focus.

The political divisions and alliances which might arise are further underlined by the fact that the new French government has come out very strongly in support of Italian participation at the start date.
Should Germany and France differ on the merits of Italy's application, Britain could hold an important swing vote and ultimately determine whether Rome qualifies.

One possible version in the calculation would have Germany voting against Italy and Britain and France for participation. All other EU countries -- except Italy which as with any other country cannot vote on its own application -- would also vote in favour, putting the total at 67.

Conversely, Italy would lose should Britain say no, all things being equal. Italy might also be excluded if Germany could secure additional support, perhaps by rallying the Netherlands and one other country to its side.
Yet some analysts and EU diplomats believe that because of the complexities and political dangers posed by the voting procedure an actual tally on membership will never come to pass.
"I don't think there will be a formal vote. That would really be a disaster," said Daniel Gros, an economist with the Centre for European Policy Studies in Brussels.

"The UK will not be active and not cast the decisive vote," he added, reckoning that an informal decision on the euro's members will be made ahead of a meeting of EU finance ministers in the spring of 1998.
But should a vote be taken, however, Britain would likely abstain, Gros said.
EU diplomats, however, caution that abstention would be equivalent to a vote against a country, complicating the issue still further.
Others say it would be political suicide for Britain to side with France and vote for Italy should Germany argue against Rome's participation.
The longer-term harm to relations between Britain and Germany would be such that the British government would likely opt for a neutral position.
